title: ICA warns of ‘disaster chasers’ posing as insurers after QLD, NSW storms
full_text:
The Insurance Council of Australia (ICA) is warning storm-hit households in Queensland and New South Wales about disaster chasers, some of whom pose as insurers. The ICA says they use that tactic to get through the door and push homeowners into unnecessary, unauthorised repair contracts.
More than 9,000 claims have been lodged since severe storms hit the two states between November 11 and 17, the ICA says.
That is up from more than 7,500 on Tuesday, when the ICA extended its Significant Event declaration (SE265). Damage has spread to the Lockyer Valley and NSW’s Mid North Coast, Hunter and Central West. Food spoilage accounts for about 27% of home claims across both states.
While insurers are on the ground supporting recovery, the ICA says opportunistic disaster chasers follow storms and take advantage of people.
Some offer tree and debris removal, hail assessments, inspections, repairs or claims management for cash upfront, then do poor work or nothing at all.
Others push homeowners to sign a contract on the spot and promise that their insurer will pay. That can leave people paying commissions or inflated bills their policy won’t cover, because insurers only pay for approved work covered by a policy.
“Sadly, disaster chasers turn up after storms to target people when they’re at their most vulnerable, and we’re now hearing some are pretending to be from insurers,” Liam Walter, ICA director, Mitigation and Extreme Weather Response, said.
“They can leave families, older Australians and vulnerable people far worse off, with big bills and homes that are still damaged.”
The ICA says anyone approached by, or who has signed with, a disaster chaser should contact their insurer. It lists five tips that brokers can pass to their clients:
“If in doubt, contact your insurer directly using the number on your policy or their official website,” Walter said.
Legal Aid Queensland says unsolicited agreements can be terminated within 10 business days without penalty.
The ICA issued a similar warning in November 2025 after southeast Queensland hailstorms. Last November’s hailstorm, declared Catastrophe 255, generated close to 99,000 claims.
ICA CEO Andrew Hall said on Tuesday that communities in both states had faced a week of severe weather. The ICA has also advised policyholders to photograph or film damage before starting a clean-up.
For brokers, the warning gives a ready checklist for clients who lodge claims or receive unsolicited offers. Brokers may also need to explain that insurers pay only for approved work covered by a policy.
Claims typically keep rising for days after an event, so client queries may continue.
author: Jonalyn Cueto
